attempts.raw_response: They can offer a safe space to explore your feelings without judgment, helping you identify patterns that keep you stuck. Once you understand the root causes, you can begin to challenge those fears. Start small—perhaps by agreeing to a casual date or a shared project. Each step forward builds confidence. Remember, commitment isn’t about losing yourself; it’s about creating space for another person while maintaining your own identity. Be patient with yourself; change takes time. With self-reflection and support, you can move toward healthier, more fulfilling connections.

pair.human_continuation: You may also consider talking with family members you consider “safe” to get more information on what took place during your childhood. Keep in mind that trauma and your age at the time of the experience may affect your memory.  You may have had a previous relationship you thought was going well end suddenly without warning. You may have been in a previous abusive relationship. You may have suffered child abuse or other trauma while growing up. You may have experienced your parents divorcing while growing up.  You may have unmet needs or attachment issues stemming from childhood. Figure out what it is about commitment that scares you. Different people may find different aspects of commitment frightening.
pair.prefix: You could also type “find a therapist” into a search engine and you will find websites that can help you locate one. A fear of commitment is likely the result of past experiences. Consider what events in your life may have contributed to your fear. A therapist or close friend may be able to help you with this by being there to listen to you.
